content: Ascaris lumbricoides is a parasitic roundworm that infects humans and can grow up to 35 cm in length, making it the largest and most common parasitic worm in humans. It causes a disease called ascariasis, which is classified as a helminthiasis and is part of the group of neglected tropical diseases. Approximately one-sixth of the global population is infected with Ascaris lumbricoides or a related roundworm, with the highest prevalence in tropical and subtropical regions. The lifecycle of Ascaris lumbricoides begins when a human ingests fertilized eggs, typically through contaminated food or water. Once ingested, the eggs hatch into larvae in the duodenum. The larvae penetrate the intestinal wall and enter the bloodstream, traveling to the liver and heart before reaching the lungs via pulmonary circulation. In the alveoli of the lungs, the larvae grow and molt. After about three weeks, the larvae migrate up the respiratory tract, are coughed up, and then swallowed, returning to the small intestine. In the intestine, the larvae mature into adult worms, which can be male or female. Female worms can produce up to 200,000 eggs per day for a year. These eggs are excreted in feces and become infectious after two weeks in soil. The eggs are highly resilient, with a lipid layer that protects them from acids, alkalis, and other chemicals, allowing them to survive in soil for over a decade. Morphologically, Ascaris lumbricoides is notable for its size. Male worms have a ventrally curved posterior end with a pointed tail, while females are larger and wider. The vulva of the female is located near the anterior end and constitutes about one-third of the body length. The uteri of a female worm can contain up to 27 million eggs at a time. Fertilized eggs are oval or round with a thick outer shell, while unfertilized eggs are slightly smaller and have a different shape. Infections with Ascaris lumbricoides are most common in areas with poor sanitation, particularly where human feces are used as fertilizer. Symptoms of infection are often absent, but in severe cases, individuals may experience bloody sputum, cough, fever, abdominal discomfort, intestinal ulcers, or the passage of worms. Ascariasis is the most common cause of Löffler's syndrome, which is characterized by pulmonary infiltration, eosinophilia, and radiographic opacities. Preventing infection requires proper hygiene and effective fecal treatment systems. The eggs of Ascaris lumbricoides are among the most resilient pathogens, second only to prions, and can survive in the environment for 1–3 years. Infection occurs when eggs are ingested, often through contaminated vegetables, fruits, or food handled by infected individuals. Bleach does not kill the eggs but can remove their sticky coating, allowing them to be rinsed away. High temperatures, such as those achieved through cooking or specialized composting methods, are required to destroy the eggs completely. The infection process begins when a person ingests food or water contaminated with unhatched eggs. The eggs hatch into juveniles in the duodenum, where they penetrate the intestinal mucosa and enter the bloodstream or lymphatic system. The larvae travel through the right side of the heart and into the lungs, where they break out of capillaries and enter the air spaces. Some larvae may become lost during migration and accumulate in other organs, causing acute tissue reactions. The larvae eventually migrate up the respiratory tract to the pharynx, where they are swallowed and return to the small intestine. Within 60–65 days of ingestion, the worms begin producing eggs in the intestine. The migration of the larvae may mimic an intermediate host, which could have been necessary for the development of ancestral forms of the parasite. Diagnosis of ascariasis is typically made by identifying the presence of worms or eggs in feces. Due to the high number of eggs produced, a diagnosis can often be made with just one or two fecal smears. Treatment involves the use of ascaricidal drugs, with mebendazole being the drug of choice. Mebendazole works by binding to tubulin in the worms' intestinal cells and body-wall muscles, disrupting their function. Other effective treatments include nitazoxanide and ivermectin.
